All of which surely helps to explain the unwieldiness of “The Sign in Sidney Brustein’s Window,” a play that we might have looked back on as an early effort if only Hansberry had lived.
Oscar Isaac and Rachel Brosnahan bring star power to Lorraine Hansberry's posthumously produced play, but the production struggles to find its footing in the modern era.
Oscar Isaac and Rachel Brosnahan lead a superb ensemble in this beautifully mounted revival

And yet, it still bursts with vivid theatrical life and provocative ideas which are as well realized as they probably could ever be in the current revival at the Brooklyn Academy of Music, also directed by Kauffman.
What struck me most of all in this second go-round with ’Sidney Brustein’ is Hansberry’s self-conscious commentary on art and artists, as if interrogating her own purpose before leaving it behind.
Oscar Isaac and Rachel Brosnahan make it worth seeing, especially for its promising but deeply flawed first act.
He is forceful when he’s not being playful.
Sidney is annoying and self-righteous and insistent he doesn’t harbor the prejudices he so clearly carries (especially towards women, including Iris).
Though Hansberry's dense, verbose play resists easy categorization, Anne Kauffman's production finds moments of clarity and connection amid the intellectual chaos.
But it is a grating snooze of a play; it ponders, meanders, stalls, and ultimately gets stuck in its own plot-free thicket of words.
It's not likely that this play will get another production any time soon nor find a finer Sidney than Oscar Isaac, so sign on whatever dotted line you need to see it.
This production makes you mourn for all the unwritten works Hansberry might have given us and wonder what she would have made of our current fractured state of disunion.
All in all, I left very entertained, and thinking that, sadly, the issues raised here still ring true 59 years later.
The work feels more like a series of scenes than an organic whole.
